title: Advanced RAG Architectures
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Advanced RAG Architectures ##### Seven failure modes, one metric A team in Bengaluru had a RAG system stuck at 71% answer accuracy. They spent five weeks on it: swapped embedding models three times, tuned chunk size across six values, tried four rerankers, upgraded the generator from `gpt-4o-mini` to `gpt-4o`. 74%. Then someone spent a day categorising 200 failures by hand. The distribution was not what anyone expected: | Failure mode | Share | |---|---| | Query needed decomposition (multi-hop) | 31% | | Answer spanned chunks that were never co-retrieved | 22% | | Query terminology differed from document terminology | 18% | | Correct chunk retrieved but ranked 8th | 12% | | Content genuinely absent from the corpus | 9% | | Correct context, generator ignored it | 5% | | Retrieval returned nothing relevant | 3% | **Only 15% of failures were the thing they had been optimising.** Chunk size and embedding model quality affect the bottom three rows. The top three — 71% of failures — needed *architectural* changes: query decomposition, parent-document retrieval, and query rewriting. Adding those three took them to 89% in eleven days. **Advanced RAG is not "better retrieval." It is a set of specific interventions targeting specific failure modes** — and you cannot choose the intervention without first knowing your failure distribution. That is the discipline this article is built around. ##### Naive, advanced, modular ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph N["Naive RAG"] N1["Query"] --> N2["Embed"] --> N3["Top-k"] --> N4["Generate"] end subgraph A["Advanced RAG"] A1["Query"] --> A2["Pre-retrieval:
rewrite, expand, route"] A2 --> A3["Hybrid retrieve"] A3 --> A4["Post-retrieval:
rerank, compress, filter"] A4 --> A5["Generate"] end subgraph M["Modular RAG"] M1["Query"] --> M2{"Router"} M2 -->|simple| M3["Direct retrieve"] M2 -->|complex| M4["Decompose → sub-queries"] M2 -->|no retrieval needed| M5["Answer directly"] M4 --> M6["Parallel retrieve"] M3 --> M7["Rerank + compress"] M6 --> M7 M7 --> M8["Generate"] M8 --> M9{"Grade answer"} M9 -->|insufficient| M2 M9 -->|good| M10["Return"] end ``` The progression is from a fixed pipeline, to a fixed pipeline with better stages, to a **graph of components with conditional routing and loops**. Modular RAG is where the top-three failure modes get addressed, because they need decisions the pipeline makes at runtime. ##### Building the failure taxonomy Do this before optimising anything. It is your assignment, and it is the highest-value day of work in this article. ```python from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict from enum import Enum class FailureMode(str, Enum): MISSING_CONTENT = "content_not_in_corpus" MISSED_TOP_K = "relevant_chunk_below_cutoff" NOT_RETRIEVED = "relevant_chunk_never_surfaced" CHUNK_FRAGMENTED = "answer_spans_uncoretrieved_chunks" VOCAB_MISMATCH = "query_terminology_differs" NEEDS_DECOMPOSITION = "multi_hop_question" CONTEXT_IGNORED = "generator_ignored_correct_context" HALLUCINATED = "generator_fabricated_despite_context" WRONG_FORMAT = "answer_correct_but_unusable" FIXES = { FailureMode.MISSING_CONTENT: "Ingest more sources; or refuse cleanly", FailureMode.MISSED_TOP_K: "Reranker; increase candidate pool", FailureMode.NOT_RETRIEVED: "Hybrid search; better embedding model", FailureMode.CHUNK_FRAGMENTED: "Parent-document or sentence-window retrieval", FailureMode.VOCAB_MISMATCH: "Query rewriting; HyDE; hybrid search", FailureMode.NEEDS_DECOMPOSITION: "Query decomposition; multi-step retrieval", FailureMode.CONTEXT_IGNORED: "Stronger prompt; reorder context; fewer chunks", FailureMode.HALLUCINATED: "Grounding checks; refusal instruction", FailureMode.WRONG_FORMAT: "Structured output (Day 18)", } @dataclass class FailureRecord: query: str expected_chunk_ids: set retrieved_chunk_ids: list answer: str mode: FailureMode note: str = "" def auto_classify(record, retrieved_ids, expected_ids, answer_correct, answer_grounded): """Partial automation — a human still reviews the ambiguous cases.""" hit = set(retrieved_ids) & expected_ids if not expected_ids: return FailureMode.MISSING_CONTENT if not hit: return FailureMode.NOT_RETRIEVED if hit and min(retrieved_ids.index(i) for i in hit) >= 5: return FailureMode.MISSED_TOP_K if len(expected_ids) > 1 and len(hit) < len(expected_ids): return FailureMode.CHUNK_FRAGMENTED if hit and not answer_correct and answer_grounded: return FailureMode.CONTEXT_IGNORED if hit and not answer_grounded: return FailureMode.HALLUCINATED return None # needs human judgement def failure_report(records): from collections import Counter counts = Counter(r.mode for r in records) total = len(records) return [{"mode": m.value, "count": c, "pct": round(100 * c / total, 1), "fix": FIXES[m]} for m, c in counts.most_common()] ``` **The `expected_chunk_ids` field is what makes this work**, and it requires labelling. For 100 queries, mark which chunks *should* be retrieved. That is a day of work and it converts guessing into engineering. ##### Pre-retrieval: query rewriting Fixes the vocabulary-mismatch mode. Users write "can't log in"; documents say "authentication failure." ```python import json from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() REWRITE_SYSTEM = """You rewrite user questions into search queries that will match technical documentation. Rules: - Expand colloquial phrasing into the formal terminology likely used in docs. - Preserve all specific identifiers exactly (error codes, clause numbers, IDs). - Keep it under 25 words. - Output only the rewritten query.""" def rewrite_query(question: str, domain_hint: str = "", model="gpt-4o-mini") -> str: r = client.chat.completions.create( model=model, temperature=0.0, max_tokens=80, messages=[ {"role": "system", "content": REWRITE_SYSTEM + (f"\n\nDomain: {domain_hint}" if domain_hint else "")}, {"role": "user", "content": question}, ], ) return r.choices[0].message.content.strip() def multi_query(question: str, n=3, model="gpt-4o-mini") -> list[str]: """Generate diverse phrasings; retrieve for all and fuse.""" r = client.chat.completions.create( model=model, temperature=0.7, response_format={"type": "json_object"}, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f'Generate {n} different search queries for this question, each ' f'emphasising a different aspect or using different terminology.\n\n' f'Question: {question}\n\n' f'Return JSON: {{"queries": ["...", "...", "..."]}}'}], ) return json.loads(r.choices[0].message.content)["queries"] ``` **Always retrieve for the original query too.** Rewriting can drift, and fusing original plus rewritten results is more robust than replacing. **Watch the latency cost.** Query rewriting adds an LLM call before retrieval — 300–800ms. For an interactive product that is significant, and it is a reason to route: rewrite only when the initial retrieval scores poorly. ##### Query decomposition The largest failure category in the Bengaluru distribution, and the one naive RAG cannot address at all. *"How does our 2026 leave policy differ from the 2024 circular?"* requires two retrievals and a comparison. One embedding of that sentence retrieves neither document well. ```python from pydantic import BaseModel from typing import Literal class SubQuery(BaseModel): query: str reason: str class Decomposition(BaseModel): needs_decomposition: bool query_type: Literal["simple", "comparison", "multi_hop", "aggregation"] sub_queries: list[SubQuery] DECOMPOSE_SYSTEM = """Decide whether a question requires multiple retrievals. needs_decomposition = true when the question: - compares two or more things - requires chaining facts (A depends on B, which must be looked up first) - aggregates across multiple documents Otherwise false, and sub_queries should be empty. Each sub-query must be independently answerable by document retrieval.""" def decompose(question: str, model="gpt-4o-mini") -> Decomposition: completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse( model=model, temperature=0.0, response_format=Decomposition, messages=[{"role": "system", "content": DECOMPOSE_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": question}], ) return completion.choices[0].message.parsed def answer_decomposed(question, retriever, generator, max_sub=4): plan = decompose(question) if not plan.needs_decomposition: chunks = retriever(question) return generator(question, chunks) sub_answers = [] all_chunks = [] for sq in plan.sub_queries[:max_sub]: chunks = retriever(sq.query) all_chunks.extend(chunks) sub_answers.append({ "question": sq.query, "answer": generator(sq.query, chunks)["answer"], }) synthesis_context = "\n\n".join( f"Sub-question: {s['question']}\nAnswer: {s['answer']}" for s in sub_answers) return generator( question, chunks=all_chunks, extra_context=f"Intermediate findings:\n{synthesis_context}", ) ``` **Cap the sub-queries.** Without a limit, a vague question decomposes into eight sub-queries and your latency and cost explode. Four is a reasonable ceiling. **Multi-hop needs sequencing**, not parallelism. "What is the notice period for the vendor who supplied our Chennai warehouse racking?" requires finding the vendor first, then their contract. Parallel retrieval fails; the second query depends on the first answer. ##### Parent-document and sentence-window retrieval Fixes the fragmentation mode — small chunks retrieve precisely but lack context; large chunks have context but retrieve fuzzily. **The resolution: embed small, return large.** ```python import uuid from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter class ParentDocumentRetriever: """Index small child chunks; return their larger parents.""" def __init__(self, vectorstore, parent_size=2400, child_size=400, overlap=60): self.vs = vectorstore self.parent_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter( chunk_size=parent_size, chunk_overlap=0) self.child_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter( chunk_size=child_size, chunk_overlap=overlap) self.parents: dict[str, str] = {} def add_documents(self, docs): child_texts, child_metas, child_ids = [], [], [] for doc in docs: for parent in self.parent_splitter.split_text(doc["text"]): pid = str(uuid.uuid4()) self.parents[pid] = parent for j, child in enumerate(self.child_splitter.split_text(parent)): child_ids.append(f"{pid}::c{j}") child_texts.append(child) child_metas.append({**doc.get("metadata", {}), "parent_id": pid}) self.vs.upsert(ids=child_ids, documents=child_texts, metadatas=child_metas) def retrieve(self, query, k=5, fetch_k=20): """Search children, deduplicate to parents, return parents.""" res = self.vs.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=fetch_k, include=["metadatas", "distances"]) seen, out = set(), [] for meta, dist in zip(res["metadatas"][0], res["distances"][0]): pid = meta["parent_id"] if pid in seen: continue seen.add(pid) out.append({"text": self.parents[pid], "score": 1 - dist, "metadata": meta}) if len(out) >= k: break return out ``` **`fetch_k` must exceed `k` substantially**, because multiple children collapse to one parent. Fetching 20 children typically yields 5–8 distinct parents. **Sentence-window retrieval** is the finer-grained variant — embed individual sentences, return the sentence plus `w` neighbours on each side: ```python def sentence_window_index(text, window=3): import re sentences = re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", text) records = [] for i, s in enumerate(sentences): lo, hi = max(0, i - window), min(len(sentences), i + window + 1) records.append({ "embed_text": s, # embed just the sentence "return_text": " ".join(sentences[lo:hi]), # return the window "metadata": {"sentence_index": i}, }) return records ``` Precise retrieval, adequate context, and cheaper than parent-document because the returned spans are smaller. ##### Post-retrieval: context compression Retrieved chunks contain relevant sentences surrounded by irrelevant ones. Compression extracts only what matters, reducing tokens and mitigating the "lost in the middle" effect. ```python COMPRESS_SYSTEM = """Extract ONLY the sentences from the context that help answer the question. Rules: - Copy sentences verbatim. Do not paraphrase or summarise. - If nothing in the context is relevant, output exactly: NO_RELEVANT_CONTENT - Preserve any numbers, dates, clause references, and identifiers exactly.""" def compress_chunk(question: str, chunk: str, model="gpt-4o-mini") -> str | None: r = client.chat.completions.create( model=model, temperature=0.0, max_tokens=400, messages=[{"role": "system", "content": COMPRESS_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": f"Question: {question}\n\nContext:\n{chunk}"}], ) out = r.choices[0].message.content.strip() return None if out == "NO_RELEVANT_CONTENT" else out def compress_context(question, chunks, max_workers=8): """Compress in parallel; drop chunks with nothing relevant.""" from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_workers) as pool: compressed = list(pool.map( lambda c: compress_chunk(question, c["text"]), chunks)) kept = [{**c, "text": comp} for c, comp in zip(chunks, compressed) if comp] orig_chars = sum(len(c["text"]) for c in chunks) new_chars = sum(len(c["text"]) for c in kept) return kept, {"chunks_before": len(chunks), "chunks_after": len(kept), "compression_ratio": round(new_chars / max(orig_chars, 1), 3)} ``` **The `NO_RELEVANT_CONTENT` escape is the valuable part.** It filters out chunks the reranker let through, and a chunk count dropping from 8 to 3 is a strong signal that your retrieval is imprecise. **Cheaper alternatives** worth trying first: embedding-based sentence filtering (score each sentence against the query, keep the top ones — no LLM call), and LLMLingua from Day 17. ##### Self-RAG and corrective RAG Two architectures that add *judgement* to the pipeline. **Self-RAG** (Asai et al., 2023) trains the model to emit reflection tokens deciding whether to retrieve, whether retrieved passages are relevant, and whether its output is supported. Powerful, but it requires fine-tuning. **Corrective RAG (CRAG)** achieves much of the benefit with a separate grader and no fine-tuning: ```python from pydantic import BaseModel from typing import Literal class RelevanceGrade(BaseModel): grade: Literal["correct", "ambiguous", "incorrect"] reason: str GRADE_SYSTEM = """Grade whether the retrieved document is relevant to the question. correct — contains information that directly answers the question ambiguous — related topic but does not clearly answer it incorrect — unrelated""" def grade_documents(question, chunks, model="gpt-4o-mini"): grades = [] for c in chunks: completion = client.beta.chat.completions.parse( model=model, temperature=0.0, response_format=RelevanceGrade, messages=[{"role": "system", "content": GRADE_SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": f"Question: {question}\n\nDocument:\n{c['text'][:1500]}"}], ) grades.append(completion.choices[0].message.parsed) return grades def corrective_rag(question, retriever, web_search, generator, min_correct=1): """Grade retrieved docs; correct the pipeline when they are inadequate.""" chunks = retriever(question, k=5) grades = grade_documents(question, chunks) correct = [c for c, g in zip(chunks, grades) if g.grade == "correct"] ambiguous = [c for c, g in zip(chunks, grades) if g.grade == "ambiguous"] if len(correct) >= min_correct: action = "use_retrieved" context = correct elif ambiguous: action = "rewrite_and_retry" rewritten = rewrite_query(question) retry_chunks = retriever(rewritten, k=5) retry_grades = grade_documents(question, retry_chunks) context = ([c for c, g in zip(retry_chunks, retry_grades) if g.grade == "correct"] or ambiguous) else: action = "external_fallback" context = web_search(question) if web_search else [] if not context: return {"answer": "I could not find this in the available sources.", "action": "refuse", "chunks": []} return {**generator(question, context), "action": action, "chunks": context} ``` **Grading costs one LLM call per chunk**, which is real latency and cost. Two mitigations: grade in parallel, and use a small model — grading relevance is much easier than answering, so `gpt-4o-mini` or a fine-tuned cross-encoder suffices. ##### Assembling a modular pipeline ```python from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass class RAGConfig: use_rewriting: bool = True use_decomposition: bool = True use_hybrid: bool = True use_reranking: bool = True use_compression: bool = False use_grading: bool = True retrieval_k: int = 5 candidate_k: int = 25 rewrite_threshold: float = 0.45 # rewrite only when scores are weak class ModularRAG: def __init__(self, retriever, reranker, generator, config: RAGConfig): self.retriever, self.reranker = retriever, reranker self.generator, self.cfg = generator, config def answer(self, question: str) -> dict: trace = {"question": question, "steps": []} if self.cfg.use_decomposition: plan = decompose(question) trace["steps"].append({"decompose": plan.query_type}) if plan.needs_decomposition: return self._answer_multi(question, plan, trace) chunks = self.retriever(question, k=self.cfg.candidate_k) # Adaptive rewriting: only when initial retrieval looks weak if self.cfg.use_rewriting and chunks and chunks[0]["score"] < self.cfg.rewrite_threshold: rewritten = rewrite_query(question) trace["steps"].append({"rewrite": rewritten}) chunks = self.retriever(rewritten, k=self.cfg.candidate_k) if self.cfg.use_reranking: chunks = self.reranker(question, chunks, top_k=self.cfg.retrieval_k) trace["steps"].append({"rerank": len(chunks)}) if self.cfg.use_grading: grades = grade_documents(question, chunks) chunks = [c for c, g in zip(chunks, grades) if g.grade != "incorrect"] trace["steps"].append({"graded_kept": len(chunks)}) if self.cfg.use_compression and chunks: chunks, stats = compress_context(question, chunks) trace["steps"].append({"compress": stats}) if not chunks: return {"answer": "I could not find this in the documents.", "trace": trace, "chunks": []} return {**self.generator(question, chunks), "trace": trace} ``` **The `trace` is not optional.** With this many conditional stages, a bad answer could originate at any of six places, and Day 42's observability point applies with force here. **The adaptive rewrite threshold** is worth highlighting — running every stage on every query is expensive and often unnecessary. Gate the expensive stages on cheap signals. ##### Measuring each addition ```python def ablation_study(eval_set, retriever, reranker, generator, base_config): """Turn each component on one at a time and measure.""" import copy results = [] variants = { "naive": RAGConfig(use_rewriting=False, use_decomposition=False, use_hybrid=False, use_reranking=False, use_grading=False), "+hybrid": RAGConfig(use_rewriting=False, use_decomposition=False, use_reranking=False, use_grading=False), "+rerank": RAGConfig(use_rewriting=False, use_decomposition=False, use_grading=False), "+rewrite": RAGConfig(use_decomposition=False, use_grading=False), "+decompose": RAGConfig(use_grading=False), "+grading": RAGConfig(), } for name, cfg in variants.items(): pipeline = ModularRAG(retriever, reranker, generator, cfg) scores = [_score(pipeline.answer(ex["q"]), ex) for ex in eval_set] import numpy as np results.append({ "variant": name, "accuracy": round(float(np.mean([s["correct"] for s in scores])), 3), "recall@5": round(float(np.mean([s["recall"] for s in scores])), 3), "p95_latency_s": round(float(np.percentile( [s["latency"] for s in scores], 95)), 2), "cost_per_query_inr": round(float(np.mean( [s["cost"] for s in scores])), 4), }) return results ``` The Bengaluru result, reconstructed: | Variant | Accuracy | recall@5 | p95 latency | ₹/query | |---|---|---|---|---| | naive | 0.71 | 0.68 | 1.4s | 0.011 | | +hybrid | 0.76 | 0.79 | 1.7s | 0.011 | | +rerank | 0.79 | 0.87 | 2.1s | 0.013 | | +rewrite | 0.82 | 0.90 | 2.9s | 0.019 | | **+decompose** | **0.88** | 0.91 | 4.6s | 0.038 | | +grading | 0.89 | 0.91 | 6.2s | 0.061 | **Decomposition is the single largest jump**, because it addressed the largest failure category. Grading adds one point for 35% more latency — a defensible thing to skip. ##### Common mistakes - **Optimising chunk size when 71% of failures are architectural** — the five wasted weeks. - **No failure taxonomy**, so improvements are guesses. - **`fetch_k = k`** in parent-document retrieval, returning too few distinct parents. - **Replacing the original query** with the rewrite instead of fusing both. - **Unbounded decomposition**, exploding cost on vague questions. - **Parallel retrieval for genuinely sequential multi-hop questions.** - **Compressing before reranking** — compress fewer, better chunks. - **Grading every chunk with a large model** when a small one or a cross-encoder suffices. - **No trace**, making a six-stage pipeline undebuggable. - **Adding every technique** rather than the ones your failures call for. - **Ignoring latency.** A 6.2-second p95 is unusable in chat regardless of accuracy. ##### Hands-on: fix the fragmentation Your practical task implements parent-document retrieval and measures the improvement over naive fixed-chunk RAG. Use `fetch_k=20, k=5` and log how many distinct parents you get — if it is consistently 2 or 3, raise `fetch_k`. Measure both recall and answer accuracy; parent-document typically improves answer quality more than it improves recall, because the win is context completeness rather than finding the right chunk. The mini project builds a modular RAG system with rewriting, reranking, and compression, benchmarked with RAGAS. Run the ablation rather than enabling everything at once — the per-component table is the deliverable, and it is what lets you argue for or against each stage on evidence. Track latency and cost alongside quality in every row. The assignment produces a failure taxonomy for a real corpus and maps each mode to a fix. Label 100–200 real queries with expected chunk IDs, run your current system, and classify every failure. Then predict which intervention should help most, implement only that one, and check whether the prediction held. That predict-then-verify loop is the difference between engineering and trial and error. ##### Key takeaways - **Build the failure taxonomy before optimising.** Chunk size and embedding quality address a minority of failures; decomposition, parent-document retrieval, and rewriting address the majority. - **Modular RAG adds routing and loops** — the conditional decisions are what handle multi-hop and vocabulary-mismatch failures that a fixed pipeline cannot. - **Embed small, return large.** Parent-document and sentence-window retrieval resolve the precision-versus-context tension directly. - **Corrective RAG grades retrieved documents and changes strategy** when they are inadequate, giving you self-correction without fine-tuning. - **Ablate every component and report latency and cost per row** — grading adding one accuracy point for 35% more latency is a decision, not an obvious win.
